# Executive summary 

As a consequence of the revisions made to both production and consumption estimates for 2012 our forecast global market surplus now stands at ~170kt with stocks at 58 days of consumption for the year.  This compares to a meagre surplus of ~43kt and stocks at 52 days of consumption in our previous LTO.  Our average price for this year is now $7946/t ($3.60/lb), marginally lower than our previous estimate of $7997/t ($3.63/lb). 

For the second consecutive LTO we begin our discussion of global copper demand by highlighting a downgrade to our global growth estimate for 2012.  Few markets have evaded cuts but the key to our lower global growth rate of 1% is a reduction in expectations for China, with a 5% expansion now estimated for this year, from 6.25% in our previous LTO. Ultimately, the recovery that we expected in the second half of the year was not of sufficient magnitude to drive the upturn that we had forecast, although at least the tentative improvements that we have seen give us greater conviction in our forecast 8.5% increase in Chinese demand next year.  This will underpin global growth of 5.1% in 2013 despite still muted consumption growth expectations for the traditional consuming regions of Europe, North America and Japan. 

Overall base case mine production capability is forecast to rise from 16.2Mt in 2011 to 21.3Mt by 2015, an increase of 32%.  Beyond 2015 mine production should decline due to reserve depletion to reach 15.7Mt by 2025.  This means that over the forecast period, base case production capability will fall at an average rate of 0.2% p.a.  We expect the market to be effectively balanced this year with primary supply exceeding demand by ~170kt, while metal from base case mines under construction and those projects currently in our ‘highly probable’ category will push the market into surplus from 2013 to 2016.  From 2017 onwards, demand for mine output should once again exceed available base case plus highly probable supply. 

Our smelter production capability forecast for 2012 is 16.3Mt, representing a 3.1% increase from 2011, although a lack of availability of concentrates and scrap are likely to moderate this increase to close to 2% in terms of actual production. Smelter output capability growth is expected to be strong next year at 12.0%, primarily as a result of increased mine feed although increasing smelter capacity in China should also contribute.  However, with the timing of some project ramp ups remaining uncertain and mines subject to disruptions, a lack of concentrates may moderate this increase to around 7% in terms of actual production.  A total of 5.1Mt of additional smelter production capability is expected over the forecast period with over half coming from China. 

The majority of the revisions made to our

smelter production capability forecasts are largely reflected in the changes to our refinery output estimates and these can be seen in the main chapter.  Taking these into account, base case global copper refined production reached 19.7Mt/a in 2011 (+3.6%), while capability is expected to increase by a further 3.0% this year, to 21.0Mt.  A 12.8% year-on-year increment will see this figure rise to 22.8Mt/a in 2013, and then to 25.1Mt in 2014.  However, growth is forecast to slow in 2015, and then to decline from 2016 onwards.  As a consequence, overall global capability will increase by only 1.6% p.a. between 2011 and 2025.  In tonnage terms this equates to an increase of ~5.0Mt to 24.6Mt in 2025. 

A weaker growth outlook for consumption over the 2013 to 2015 period combined with the new supply that we forecast will result in a surplus remaining in place over the coming years.  The increase to our disruption allowance from 2013 onwards will limit next year’s surplus to just ~260kt with stocks edging up slightly to 60 days of consumption.  Prices are expected to trade slightly lower to $7500/t ($3.50/lb) in 2012$ in line with rising inventories.  Over the period 2014 to 2016, we expect further downward pressure on prices in tandem with a further ongoing build in metal inventories, with stock days to consumption moving above 80 and a commensurate reduction in prices by 2017 to a low of $5401/t ($2.45/lb) in 2012$. 

Under these circumstances it is inevitable that there will be a supply side response to the lower prices and this will manifest itself in a period of weaker capital investment.  This will lead to slower production growth which will ultimately bring the market back into balance.  Beyond then, projected market deficits over the period 2018-2020 should see prices moving back to our forecast long-term incentive level of $6614/t ($3.00/lb) in constant 2012$.

Although we finally began to see the first tangible signs of an upturn in copper wire and cable demand in November, the impact on the copper rod business has not been as great as anticipated. Due to weaker demand from end users, wire and cable production slowed in October from the higher levels that had been seen in August and September. Faced with the lack of follow through orders, a number of the smaller and mid-sized rod mills chose to idle their lines through the October national holiday week, leading to a decline in average industry utilisation. High copper prices of RMB59,000/mt, coupled with pessimism over the short term outlook, and the knowledge that some downstream consumers were also shutting down their operations for the holidays also contributed to the negative short term view. The weakness of the market also led to the suspension of production at Xiangrui’s new 300kta capacity rod mill due to the lack of orders. The disappointment of October meant that our 6.25% view for the full year outlook for refined consumption was no longer realistically achievable and we have downgraded our growth projection to 5% in consequence. **But a November rebound in wire and cable and wire rod** November registered the first meaningful signs of a general upturn in Chinese market activity. There was a distinct increase in orders for both power cab

le and winding wire, two of the largest volume product lines in the Chinese market, suggesting that a broad based improvement may at last be gaining some momentum. Utilisation rates in the wire and cable industry reached their highest level so far this year at just under 80%, compared to 71% in the early part of the year. Although there is some evidence that the stimulus measures announced earlier this year may be starting to take effect, there is also the belief that the widespread industry destocking of final inventories may be coming to an end, enabling new orders to be placed to refill the supply chain pipeline. Power cable demand has benefitted recently from some strong sequential gains in power grid investment. Expenditure surged by 32% month-on-month in September, followed by a 36% month-on-month increase in October. This is in response to the release of orders after the fifth round of bidding for power cables contracts from the State Power Grid in late-September. The improvement in winding wire demand is due to a combination of continuing healthy orders from the automotive sector and an acceleration in offtake from the home appliance sector now that the worst effects of finished inventory overhang appear to be past. The clearest evidence for this is to be found in the HVACR Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - December 2012 Page 5 of 35 Copper Long Term Outlook industry where final stocks fell below monthly production in October. The increase in wire and cable production led to a 5-10% sequential monthly increase in wire rod output according to a sample of individual mill’s production plans. For those mills that shut for one week in October the increase was closer to 10-15%. A recent survey of rod producers confirmed that average capacity utilisation rose from 69% in October to 74% in November. ##### **Chinese production of copper and copper alloy products - (kt)** 40 3500

**Other product segments are stable but should improve in 2013** Despite the recent double digit increases in floor space under construction and completions, Chinese building wire consumption was reported to be stable in October and November. Cold weather is now beginning to affect construction activity in the northern provinces and this will progressively restrict sales in those regions until March. Copper tube and pipe consumption has been on a declining trend since May and fell further in October as a result of shutdowns at air conditioner plants for the national holidays. However, there is much more optimism for the year ahead with industry leader Golden Dragon projecting a 13.4% r

ebound in its tube production to 400kt in 2013 after an expected 5.4% decline to 350kt in 2012. The company expects an improvement in domestic demand as well as increased export orders to Japan, South East Asia and Europe. Golden Dragon had been forced to cut its inventories of refined copper and finished products to ease the financing burden of its working capital requirements. Sheet and strip consumption for high end sophisticated products in phosphor bronze and complex alloys has strengthened but demand for standard coppers and brasses for leadframes and connectors is stable. **Total consumption to outstrip refined** The outlook for the construction sector in particular looks positive for 2013 and beyond in the wake of the strong growth in housing starts which began in the final part of 2011. This should start to breathe some life into demand for building wire and therefore wire rod in the coming year. However, set against these positive fundamentals is the likely ramp up of commercial production at the 100% scrap fed SDI La Farga rod mill in Indiana. Assuming that quality testing with customers is successful, output from this 80k/ta line will take market share from other producers, such that even in an expanding rod market, overall growth in cathode consumption could be muted. We expect that the expansion of rod output will not only displace domestic producers but also some imports and this is a key reason for our forecast of a decline in refined demand in Canada in 2013. For 2013 we forecast only relatively modest growth in the US of 2.2%, while the expected 6.7% decline in Canadian demand results in North American refined consumption rising by 1.5% overall. This upturn in refined demand is much more sedate then the forecast increase in total copper consumption, which is set to rise by closer to 4% as a result of the increased output at SDI La Farga. This also leads to a sharp increase in the direct use of scrap in the US in 2013. ##### **North American refined copper consumption – kt** |||||||||**202**

Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - December 2012 Page 7 of 35 Copper Long Term Outlook **Latin American growth to average 3.9% over the long term** The Latin American region is enjoying a steady if unspectacular recovery from the contraction of 2011, although the positive long term outlook is undiminished. Brazil remains the engine of future regional growth because its large manufacturing base will also serve the regional economy. This will drive domestic growth in copper semis production, which, over the course of the next few years, will be boosted by investment in semis capacity. The outlook for the other regional major, Mexico, is also relatively bullish, although to a lesser extent than in Brazil. While Brazilian demand is ultimately closely tied to robust Latin American economic conditions, Mexico has a high dependence on the United States, which is the destination for around 90% of its exports of wire and cable. One of the key premises of our bearish long term forecast in the US is that it will lose out to cheaper imports of semis and finished goods and given its location, Mexico is one of the countries primed to benefit from its relative competitiveness. ##### **Latin American refined copper consumption – kt** |||||||||**202**

The prolonged nature of the regional debt crisis and its sapping effect on confidence ultimately hit the twin drivers of growth, capital investment and consumer spending. Against this already negative backdrop, austerity measures have also tempered government investment in infrastructure. These factors combined to drag consumption sharply lower. Since our last Long Term Outlook, we have, however, upgraded our European estimate and we now expect a contraction of 6.4% in 2012 compared to 7.1% previously. Ultimately, this is a result of an upgrade to Italian consumption following stronger than expected semis

output in the second half of the year. 

**Flat long term outlook masks significant differences by country** Our medium term forecasts for the region point to a recovery in demand as economic activity resumes a more normal trajectory and industrial production gradually recovers. This will result in average regional demand growth of 2.2% through the period 2013 to 2016, although the outlook beyond this is less bright, with little to no overall increase in the consumption forecast.  The total European figure does mask differences though, with Eastern European countries such as Poland and Russia still forecast to expand during the latter decade of our forecast period, although this will be offset by contraction across the traditional consuming countries in Western Europe. 

**A growing need for grid investment** The overall bearish tone to our forecast obscures some positive underlying drivers of demand in Europe.  In particular, there is a significant requirement for investment in the power grid across much of the region for two key reasons.  Firstly, the current infrastructure is relatively old in many countries and requires updating, while secondly, the current focus on renewable energy is leading to a decentralisation of the electrical grid which is also increasing the need for supporting infrastructure.  For instance, off-shore wind farms need to be connected to the grid and given their often remote locations this necessitates significant volumes of under sea cabling.  Meanwhile, there are a number of projects that have been muted to improve or establish connections between grids within the region.  This paints a positive medium to long term outlook for demand from the electrical sector, although growth expectations are tempered by the increasing threat of substitution by aluminium in power cable. 

**Sluggish is best that can be hoped for construction** Construction does not share the underlying positive outlook of the electrical sector and will be a major drag on copper demand through the short to medium term.  Our forecasts indicate no growth at all in overall construction activity in Western Europe until 2015 and from then on we do not anticipate average growth in building exceeding 1% per year.  Clearly, this will translate into continued weakness in the short to medium term and then at best sluggish growth in sectoral demand for copper over the latter stages of our forecast period. 

**Increasing Cu content to support transport growth** The outlook for the automotive sector is mixed, with steady growth expected over the longer term in Eastern Europe but little to no expansion in the traditional producing countries in Western Europe.  The short to medium term outlook is better for Western Europe with robust growth in output forecast out to 2015. **Automotive to skid from 2014** The automotive sector has grown strongly this year, in part owing to the favourable comparison with 2011 when production was disrupted by the earthquake and tsunami. Production was also driven by car purchase incentives, although when these expired in September registrations and output quickly fell away, with an attendant decline in sectoral demand. An improving environment for exports of Japanese cars will lead to further production growth in 2013 but from 2014 and beyond we anticipate that production will begin a decline that will continue virtually unabated throughout our forecast period caused by the same competitive pressures described above. This decline w

ill be countered to a degree by an increase in the copper content of vehicles as hybrid and electric vehicles take a greater share and as more functionality is added to cars. Overall, we expect little or no growth from sectoral demand through the forecast period as a whole. **Short to medium term boost for construction** Demand from the construction sector has also grown this year, although at a much slower pace than in autos, while we also anticipate a further increase in 2013 and 2014. We foresee construction activity declining over the longer term as a result of demographic shifts that will limit building activity. In contrast, the electrical infrastructure sector has been weak this year although its medium term outlook is much brighter. Following the tsunami and earthquake in March 2011, nuclear power stations were shut down en masse, with the result Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - December 2012 Page 9 of 35 Copper Long Term Outlook that power companies had to generate electricity from other sources and this was typically met by importing fossil fuels. Owing to the higher costs of these imports, energy producers had to cut back elsewhere and infrastructure investment suffered, which led to a decline in demand for copper cables from this key sector. This does suggest that there is likely to be some pent up demand from the sector which will buoy consumption in the medium term but over the longer run a declining industrial base suggests lower energy consumption, which is likely to lead to negative growth in the latter part of our forecast period. ##### **Japanese refined copper consumption – kt** |||||||||**202**

Fundamentally, it is the declining requirement by near neighbours for exports of Korean wire rod that is hitting cathode demand and with the majority of these headed for China this trend is unlikely to change. There has been a major expansion of Chinese rod capacity over the past few years and this is set to continue given a further raft of announcements over the past year. As a result of this, China will require less rod from Korea but significantly, the prospects are also raised of Chinese exports of rod into Korea displacing some domestic production and also taking a share of other export markets. The underlying demand situation is not as downbeat as for cathode, with wire and cable makers managing to maintai

n exports relatively well for now. Given that around a third of Korean exports of wire and cable head to China, the longer term outlook is less clear. Disruptions since last quarter’s LTO mean that the our 5% generic disruption allowance for 2012 set at the start of the year has now been exceeded and copper mine production capability (before any further disruptions) now stands at 16.7Mt.  Despite being down on previous estimates, this figure still represents a significant change from the low growth achieved during the past decade where exp

anding African and Chinese production has been offset by a declining contribution from North America and general stagnation in Latin America, Europe and Oceania. 

The projected 3.3% increase in year-on-year mine production capability for 2012 marks the start of a four-year growth period that should see global capability exceed 20Mt for the first time.  The commissioning of both greenfield and brownfield expansion projects in Zambia and the DRC will result in a 65% surge in African output from 2012 to 2015, a figure almost matched by a forecast 59% increase in Asia over the same period resulting largely from the start-up of Oyu Tolgoi and an expected production spike at Grasberg.  Production growth is also expected from China (13%), Middle East (16%), North America (21%), Europe (12%) and Oceania (7%), while in Latin America (25%) growth will be equivalent to 1.9Mt of additional mine production. 

The increase in production between 2013 and 2015 comes from the commissioning of new projects such as Oyu Tolgoi, Salobo, Toromocho, Ministro Mina Hales and Sierra Gorda plus the ramp up of expansions at mines such as Los Bronces, KOV and Antamina and improved performance at existing large producers such as Escondida, Collahuasi and Grasberg. 

It should be noted that this projected growth comes from our “base case” scenario only.  A further 109kt could come from “highly probable” and “probable” projects in 2013 and an additional 284kt in 2014. 

Disruptions since last quarter’s LTO have included a shortfall in overall production due to lower than forecast head grades and ongoing operational issues at some major producers.  These have been covered in more detail in our monthly updates.  Production so far this year has not been interrupted by industrial action to the same extent as during 2011 and since our last update major producers such as Andina and Anglo American Sur have negotiated new labour contracts with unions.  However, with contracts set to expire at other mines including Chuquicamata and Escondida during the first half of 2013, the risk remains that disruptions due to industrial action could hit global mine output in the short to medium term.  With a number of new mines currently in construction and forecast to commence production over the next few years, slower than expected project ramp-ups are likely to become a significant contributor to production falling short of forecasts over the next few years. 

Disruptions will undoubtedly have a negative effect on global supply on a regional basis and since our last LTO we have increased our disruption allowance for future years from 5% to 6% of forecast production capability.  However, the scale of the near-term base case project pipeline together with “highly probable” projects lead us to forecast the metal market moving into a surplus from 2012 to 2017.  From 2017 onwards increased demand and attrition at existing mines will mean that the primary market will return to a deficit condition unles

s mine projects currently in our ‘probable’ or ‘possible’ categories are developed.

We expect the market to be effectively balanced this year with primary supply exceeding demand by ~170kt, while metal from base case mines under construction and those projects currently in our ‘highly probable’ category will push the market into surplus from 2013 to 2016. 

From 2017 onwards, demand for mine output should once again exceed available base case plus highly probable supply.  This shortfall will be satisfied either by the reactivation of closed mines, new ore discoveries at currently producing mines, incremental expansions, mine life extensions or the development of greenfield projects.  Highly probable, probable and possible projects have been selected based upon various criteria, including stage of advancement, potential project returns, technical impediments, country risk, company strategy and the ability of the owner to raise finance.

In reality, the actual make up of projects developed will be a combination of these aforementioned categories plus so-called currently ‘off-radar’ projects and from a small proportion of projects in our possible category. New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not considered a new source of copper supply. A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of sc

rap as clippings, trimmings, stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-based products into finished articles.  New scrap is termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is considered to be a “new” source of supply. 

## Scrapping rates 

The availability of _old_ copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; and in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to the market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 

Over the past 20 years, the volume of _new_ copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the period. 

## Scrap usage 

Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 

Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 90-95% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities (typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment. Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode purchases. 

Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 l

ed to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentratesmelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. 

## Scrap consumption 

Copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) amounted to 8.33Mt in 2011, an increase of 4.3% on the prior year and accounting for 34% of copper consumed.  Direct use scrap took the lions share, representing some 57% of copper produced from scrap, with smelters (27%) and refineries (16%) producing copper from the balance. 

Growth in scrap use slowed in 2011 following the strong recovery in 2010, as a slowdown in the rate of price increase resulted slowed the relative increase in incentive to collect scrap while sluggish industrial production also limited scrap generation. Metals Market Service Long Term Outlook - December 2012 Page 32 of 35 Copper Long Term Outlook # Principal uses of copper Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and copper alloy products. Copper wire rod, which accounts for an estimated 55% of total Global consumption (i.e. including scrap) and ~70% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use. With the exception of silver, copper has the highest electrical conductivity of all the metals. This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and cable. Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire. In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products. Of these, construction is one of the largest sectors for consuming copper, accounting for 31% of total copper consumption. The main wire and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products. Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption. Rising intensity of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this position. The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building. In addition, recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future. One of these issues, electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper conductors. Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable segments. However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power distribution grids worldwide, still has con

siderable potential to carry energy better and reduce losses than aluminium. 

Copper tube, which accounts for an estimated 13% of global refined copper consumption, is the largest of the copper product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand growth, however, this is being offset by substitution to plastic tubing where this is possible.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort. 

Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross contamination. 

Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 34% of total copper demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, transformer windings, semiconductors, connectors and motors for heavy appliances. 

Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance networks.  However, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main network and consumers. In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried more quickly along the telecommunication network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than an analogue dial-up connection. 

Dramatic gains in copper consumption to have occurred within the home and office because of a system known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television signals is connected to a

central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable of carrying more electronic signals with less interference and resistance than the older four-stranded telephone wires. High-speed digital service lines now provide computer data transmission 50 to 270 times faster than that of the fastest dial-up modem connected to a telephone line.  More importantly, with the number of homes connected to the Internet and usage continuing to increase strongly, demand for higher quality copper telecommunication wire and cable is expected to surge in the coming years. 

The other main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  Winding wire demand accounts for an estimated 20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical goods as disposable incomes rise. 

Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 13% of total consumption. Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930, copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anticorrosi

on characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing. However, mass auto production in the 1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost. Although this form of tubing is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping. Likewise, new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector. Over the years the number of electrical and electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness). Many of the electrical components will have to be redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge. Such examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being added. Meanwhile, the introduction of electric and hybrid vehicles will also increase demand for copper from this sector as they typically have a much higher copper content than traditional vehicles because of the amount of copper in batteries among other components. Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper required per component. Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products. Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 9% of total copper consumption. The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military and civilian ordnance and coinage. The production of the Euro coin and the US presidential dollar coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products. However, copper’s use in coinage is now falling as national mints are beginning to respecify the composition of their coins to eliminate or reduce the copper content due to the rising cost of copper. This adjustment is defined as that which is required to maintain an orderly market balance and is split into two categories in order to distinguish disruption allowances from closures/reactivations on account of price/market-related conditions. The “disruption allowance” moving forward is assumed to be 5% of the production capability projection at the start of each year. As in the past, this generic figure declines as the current year progresses in tandem with the allocation of mine-specific disruptions as they become known. With regard to the “price/market adjustment”, a negative adjustment implies that mine production needs to be lost (after allowing for highly-probable new projects, incremental expansions etc.) and vice-versa. A positive adjustment could be met either by new projects, incremental expansions or extensions to the mine-life of existing operations where closure is anticipated within the forecast period due to reserve depletions. These adjustments are made on an iterative basis, and are driven by the consumption forecast. These forecasts take into account the likely level of metal prices required to affect them, as well as the impact of changes in metal stocks on metal prices. Thus, during periods of surplus supplies, metal prices need to fall to a level sufficiently low to effect the closure of marginal mine capacity.
